### How to use this guide

- Every sub-topic follows the same four-part pattern: **What it is** (a one-line definition), **How to identify it** (the wording or pattern that tells you which method to reach for), **How to solve it** (the method, with the key formulas), and **two worked examples**.
- Learn to **identify first**. Most lost marks in aptitude tests come from choosing the wrong method, not from calculation slips. Read the identify bullets before the solve steps.
- Figure-based reasoning questions (mirror images, paper folding, figure series) are described in words and symbols here. The method is the same on the real figures; practise those on paper too.
- Suggested routine: read one sub-topic, cover the solutions, solve both examples yourself, then compare. Then do 10 fresh questions from any practice book on the same sub-topic.
- Time targets for most company placement tests: quantitative about 1 minute per question, reasoning about 1 minute, verbal 45 to 60 seconds, data interpretation 1.5 to 2 minutes. Skip anything that crosses double the target and return to it at the end.
- Formulas are written in plain text: x² means x squared, aₙ means the n-th term, × is multiplication, ÷ is division and √ is the square root.

#### 1.1.1 Types of numbers

**What it is:** Numbers are grouped by their properties: natural (1, 2, 3, …), whole (0, 1, 2, …), integers (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …), rational (can be written as p/q), irrational (non-terminating, non-repeating decimals such as √2 and π), prime (exactly two factors) and composite (more than two factors).

**How to identify it**

- The question uses words like prime, composite, co-prime, rational, irrational, perfect number, consecutive.
- "How many primes between…", "smallest composite number", "sum of first n natural numbers".

**How to solve it**

- To test if n is prime, divide by every prime up to √n. If none divides it, n is prime.
- 1 is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime.
- Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2. Sum of first n odd numbers = n². Sum of first n even numbers = n(n+1).
- Co-prime numbers have HCF 1 and need not be prime themselves (8 and 15 are co-prime).

**Example 1.** Is 221 prime? **Solution.** √221 is about 14.9, so test primes up to 13. 221 ÷ 13 = 17 exactly, so 221 = 13 × 17. It is composite.

**Example 2.** Find the sum of all odd numbers from 1 to 49. **Solution.** Odd numbers from 1 to 49 are the first 25 odd numbers, because 49 = 2 × 25 − 1. Sum = 25² = 625.

#### 1.1.2 Divisibility rules

**What it is:** Quick tests that tell whether a number divides another exactly, without carrying out the division.

**How to identify it**

- "Find the digit \* so that the number is divisible by…", "which of these is divisible by…".
- "Smallest number to add or subtract to make it divisible by…".

**How to solve it**

- 2: last digit even. 3: digit sum divisible by 3. 4: last two digits divisible by 4. 5: last digit 0 or 5.
- 8: last three digits divisible by 8. 9: digit sum divisible by 9. 10: last digit 0.
- 11: (sum of digits in odd places) − (sum of digits in even places) is 0 or a multiple of 11.
- 7: remove the last digit, subtract twice that digit from the rest, repeat until small.
- For composite divisors test co-prime parts: 6 = 2 × 3, 12 = 3 × 4, 72 = 8 × 9.

**Example 1.** Find the digit x so that 4x56 is divisible by 9. **Solution.** Digit sum = 4 + x + 5 + 6 = 15 + x. The next multiple of 9 after 15 is 18, so x = 3. Check: 4356 ÷ 9 = 484.

**Example 2.** Is 918082 divisible by 11? **Solution.** Digits from the left: 9, 1, 8, 0, 8, 2. Odd places (1st, 3rd, 5th): 9 + 8 + 8 = 25. Even places: 1 + 0 + 2 = 3. Difference = 22, a multiple of 11, so yes. (918082 ÷ 11 = 83462.)

#### 1.1.3 HCF & LCM

**What it is:** The HCF is the greatest number that divides every given number exactly. The LCM is the smallest number that every given number divides exactly.

**How to identify it**

- HCF situations (splitting): greatest number that divides, largest tile, longest rope that measures exactly, maximum number of equal groups.
- LCM situations (meeting again): bells ringing together, runners meeting at the start, smallest number divisible by all, "after how much time together again".

**How to solve it**

- Prime factorise. HCF = product of the lowest powers of common primes. LCM = product of the highest powers of all primes.
- For two numbers: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
- Greatest number that divides a, b, c leaving remainders r₁, r₂, r₃ = HCF of (a − r₁), (b − r₂), (c − r₃).
- Smallest number leaving the same remainder r on division by several numbers = LCM + r.
- Fractions: HCF = HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators. LCM = LCM of numerators ÷ HCF of denominators.

**Example 1.** Find the greatest number that divides 285 and 1249 leaving remainders 9 and 7 respectively. **Solution.** Subtract the remainders: 285 − 9 = 276 and 1249 − 7 = 1242. HCF(276, 1242): 1242 = 4 × 276 + 138, and 276 = 2 × 138, so the HCF is 138. 138 is larger than both remainders, so it is valid.

**Example 2.** Three bells ring every 12, 15 and 20 minutes. They ring together at 8:00 a.m. When next together? **Solution.** 12 = 2² × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 20 = 2² × 5. LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60 minutes, so they ring together next at 9:00 a.m.

#### 1.1.4 Factors & multiples

**What it is:** Factors of a number divide it exactly; multiples are obtained by multiplying it by whole numbers. Counting factors is done from the prime factorisation.

**How to identify it**

- "How many factors/divisors", "sum of all factors", "product of factors".
- "In how many ways can N be written as a product of two numbers", "number of odd factors", "perfect square".

**How to solve it**

- Write N = aᵖ × b^q × cʳ (primes a, b, c).
- Number of factors = (p+1)(q+1)(r+1).
- Sum of factors = (aᵖ⁺¹ − 1)/(a − 1) × (b^q⁺¹ − 1)/(b − 1) × (cʳ⁺¹ − 1)/(c − 1).
- Ways to write N as a product of two different factors = (number of factors) ÷ 2 if N is not a perfect square, or (number of factors − 1) ÷ 2 if it is.
- N is a perfect square exactly when every exponent is even (so it has an odd number of factors).
- For odd factors, ignore the prime 2 in the count.

**Example 1.** How many factors does 360 have, and what is their sum? **Solution.** 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Number of factors = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Sum = (2⁴ − 1)/1 × (3³ − 1)/2 × (5² − 1)/4 = 15 × 13 × 6 = 1170.

**Example 2.** In how many ways can 144 be written as a product of two different factors? **Solution.** 144 = 2⁴ × 3², so it has 5 × 3 = 15 factors. It is a perfect square. Ways = (15 − 1) ÷ 2 = 7. They are 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, 4×36, 6×24, 8×18, 9×16.

#### 1.1.5 Remainders

**What it is:** Finding what is left when a number, often a huge power or product, is divided by another number.

**How to identify it**

- "Remainder when … is divided by …", especially with large powers, products, or factorial sums.
- "Last two digits" is the remainder on division by 100.

**How to solve it**

- Remainder of a sum or product = sum or product of the individual remainders, reduced again.
- Use negative remainders to shrink numbers: 99 ≡ −1 (mod 100), 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11).
- For powers, list the remainders until they repeat, then use the exponent modulo the cycle length.
- Fermat: if p is prime and a is not a multiple of p, then aᵖ⁻¹ leaves remainder 1 on division by p.
- Wilson: (p − 1)! leaves remainder p − 1 on division by p, for prime p.
- n! is divisible by every number up to n, so most terms of a factorial sum vanish.

**Example 1.** Find the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7. **Solution.** Powers of 2 leave remainders 2, 4, 1 and then repeat (cycle length 3). 100 = 3 × 33 + 1, so 2¹⁰⁰ leaves the same remainder as 2¹, which is 2.

**Example 2.** Find the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50! is divided by 12. **Solution.** From 4! = 24 onward, every factorial is divisible by 12. So the remainder is that of 1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9. Remainder = 9.

#### 1.1.6 Unit digit & cyclicity

**What it is:** The last digit of aⁿ repeats in a short cycle that depends only on the last digit of a.

**How to identify it**

- "Unit digit of 7¹²³", "last digit of a product or sum of powers".
- Power towers, such as 3 raised to (4 raised to 5), need care with the exponent.

**How to solve it**

- Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 never change. Last digit 4 and 9 cycle with length 2 (4, 6 and 9, 1).
- Last digit 2, 3, 7, 8 cycle with length 4: 2→2,4,8,6; 3→3,9,7,1; 7→7,9,3,1; 8→8,4,2,6.
- Divide the exponent by the cycle length. The remainder picks the term; remainder 0 means the last term of the cycle.
- Multiply the unit digits of the separate parts and keep only the last digit.
- Power tower: work from the top. Find the remainder of the upper exponent on division by the cycle length (4 for 2, 3, 7, 8), then use that as the exponent of the base.

**Example 1.** Find the unit digit of 7⁹⁵. **Solution.** The cycle for 7 is 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4). 95 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 3, so take the third term: 3.

**Example 2.** Find the unit digit of (234)¹⁰⁰ × (567)¹⁰¹. **Solution.** Unit digit of 4¹⁰⁰: even exponent gives 6. Unit digit of 7¹⁰¹: 101 ÷ 4 leaves 1, so 7. 6 × 7 = 42, so the unit digit is 2.

#### 1.1.7 Factorials & trailing zeros

**What it is:** n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × … × n. Each trailing zero needs a factor pair 2 × 5, and fives are scarcer than twos.

**How to identify it**

- "Number of zeros at the end of n!", "highest power of p that divides n!".
- "Largest power of 12 (or 6, 10) dividing n!".

**How to solve it**

- Zeros in n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … (keep dividing and take whole parts).
- Highest power of a prime p in n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + ….
- For a composite divisor, split into primes, find each prime's power, and take the limiting one (divide by the exponent in the divisor).

**Example 1.** How many zeros are at the end of 100!? **Solution.** 100 ÷ 5 = 20, 100 ÷ 25 = 4, 100 ÷ 125 = 0. Zeros = 20 + 4 = 24.

**Example 2.** Find the highest power of 6 that divides 20!. **Solution.** 6 = 2 × 3. Power of 3 in 20! = ⌊20/3⌋ + ⌊20/9⌋ = 6 + 2 = 8. Power of 2 in 20! = 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18, which is more than enough. The limiting prime is 3, so the answer is 6⁸.

#### 1.1.8 Number base systems

**What it is:** A base-b system uses b digits. Common bases are 2 (binary), 8 (octal), 10 (decimal) and 16 (hexadecimal, digits 0–9 and A–F where A = 10 … F = 15).

**How to identify it**

- Numbers written with a subscript base such as (1011)₂.
- "Convert", "in base 5", "binary addition", "hexadecimal".

**How to solve it**

- Base b to decimal: multiply each digit by the matching power of b and add.
- Decimal to base b: divide repeatedly by b and read the remainders from the last to the first.
- Binary to octal: group bits in threes from the right. Binary to hex: group in fours.
- Arithmetic in base b is ordinary arithmetic, but you carry when a column reaches b.

**Example 1.** Convert 156 to binary. **Solution.** 156 ÷ 2 = 78 r0, 78 ÷ 2 = 39 r0, 39 ÷ 2 = 19 r1, 19 ÷ 2 = 9 r1, 9 ÷ 2 = 4 r1, 4 ÷ 2 = 2 r0, 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r0, 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r1. Reading remainders from bottom to top: 10011100. Check: 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 156.

**Example 2.** Add (1011)₂ and (110)₂ and give the answer in decimal. **Solution.** 1011 + 0110: column by column with carries gives 10001. In decimal: 11 + 6 = 17, and (10001)₂ = 16 + 1 = 17.

#### 1.1.9 Surds & indices

**What it is:** Indices (powers) show repeated multiplication. Surds are irrational roots such as √3 that cannot be simplified to whole numbers or fractions.

**How to identify it**

- Equations with the unknown in the power: "if 4ˣ⁺¹ = 8ˣ⁻¹, find x".
- Expressions with roots to simplify or rationalise.

**How to solve it**

- Laws: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a¹/ⁿ is the n-th root of a.
- If the bases are equal, equate the exponents. Rewrite numbers to a common base first (8 = 2³, 9 = 3²).
- Rationalise: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. 1/(√a − √b) = (√a + √b)/(a − b).
- Only like surds add or subtract: 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3, but √2 + √3 stays as it is.

**Example 1.** Solve 4ˣ⁺¹ = 8ˣ⁻¹. **Solution.** Write both with base 2: 2²⁽ˣ⁺¹⁾ = 2³⁽ˣ⁻¹⁾. So 2x + 2 = 3x − 3, which gives x = 5.

**Example 2.** Rationalise 1/(√5 − √3). **Solution.** Multiply top and bottom by (√5 + √3). Result = (√5 + √3)/(5 − 3) = (√5 + √3)/2.

#### 1.1.10 Logarithms

**What it is:** log\_b N = x means bˣ = N. A logarithm is the power to which the base must be raised to get the number.

**How to identify it**

- The word "log" or "log to the base", equations like log₂ x = 5.
- "How many digits does 2⁵⁰ have" (given log 2).

**How to solve it**

- log(mn) = log m + log n; log(m/n) = log m − log n; log(mⁿ) = n log m.
- log\_b b = 1, log\_b 1 = 0, log\_b a = 1 / logₐ b, and change of base: log\_b a = log a / log b.
- Convert a log equation into its power form to solve it.
- Number of digits in N = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1.

**Example 1.** Evaluate log₂ 64 + log₃ 81 − log₅ 125. **Solution.** 2⁶ = 64 gives 6. 3⁴ = 81 gives 4. 5³ = 125 gives 3. Total = 6 + 4 − 3 = 7.

**Example 2.** Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, find the number of digits in 2⁵⁰. **Solution.** log₁₀(2⁵⁰) = 50 × 0.3010 = 15.05. Digits = ⌊15.05⌋ + 1 = 16.

#### 1.2.1 BODMAS

**What it is:** The agreed order for evaluating an expression: Brackets, Orders (powers and roots), Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction.

**How to identify it**

- A long expression mixing brackets, powers, ×, ÷, + and −; "find the value of".

**How to solve it**

- Open brackets from the innermost: ( ) first, then { }, then \[ \].
- Next powers and roots. Then division and multiplication together, working left to right.
- Finally addition and subtraction together, left to right.
- "Of" means multiplication and is done before ordinary division and multiplication.

**Example 1.** Evaluate 48 ÷ 6 × 2 + 3² − (10 − 4). **Solution.** Brackets: 10 − 4 = 6. Orders: 3² = 9. Division and multiplication left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16. Then 16 + 9 − 6 = 19.

**Example 2.** Evaluate 15 − \[4 + {6 − (3 − 1)}\] ÷ 2. **Solution.** Innermost: (3 − 1) = 2. Then {6 − 2} = 4. Then \[4 + 4\] = 8. 8 ÷ 2 = 4, and 15 − 4 = 11.

#### 1.2.2 Fractions & decimals

**What it is:** Converting between fractions and decimals, comparing them, and doing arithmetic with them, including recurring decimals.

**How to identify it**

- Mixed fractions, recurring decimals such as 0.(36), "arrange in ascending order", "which is greater".

**How to solve it**

- Pure recurring: 0.(ab) = ab/99 and 0.(a) = a/9.
- Mixed recurring: 0.a(b) = (ab − a)/90. For example 0.1(6) = (16 − 1)/90 = 1/6.
- Compare fractions by cross-multiplying or by converting to decimals.
- Learn: 1/3 = 0.333, 1/6 = 0.1667, 1/7 = 0.142857, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/9 = 0.111, 1/11 = 0.0909.

**Example 1.** Convert 0.(36) into a fraction. **Solution.** 0.(36) = 36/99. Divide top and bottom by 9: 4/11. **Example 2.** Arrange 3/4, 5/7 and 7/9 in ascending order. **Solution.** 3/4 = 0.75, 5/7 = 0.714, 7/9 = 0.778. Ascending order: 5/7, 3/4, 7/9.

#### 1.2.3 Squares, cubes & roots

**What it is:** Fast mental methods for squaring, cubing and taking roots, which save time in simplification questions.

**How to identify it**

- "Find the value of 47²", "√7569", "cube root of 17576", or any simplification built on perfect squares and cubes.

**How to solve it**

- Square via a nearby round number: 47² = (47 + 3)(47 − 3) + 3² = 50 × 44 + 9 = 2209.
- Numbers ending in 5: for n5, the square is n(n+1) followed by 25 (65² = 4225).
- Square root: squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9. Use nearby perfect squares to get the tens digit, the last digit to choose between two candidates.
- Cube root of a perfect cube (up to 6 digits): the last digit of the cube fixes the last digit of the root (1→1, 2→8, 3→7, 4→4, 5→5, 6→6, 7→3, 8→2, 9→9). The leading digits, compared with 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, fix the tens digit.

**Example 1.** Find √7569. **Solution.** 80² = 6400 and 90² = 8100, so the root is between 80 and 90. The number ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7. 85² = 7225 is less than 7569, so the root is above 85. The root is 87 (87² = 7569).

**Example 2.** Find the cube root of 17576. **Solution.** The last digit is 6, so the root ends in 6. Remove the last three digits to leave 17. Since 8 ≤ 17 \< 27, the tens digit is 2. Root = 26. Check: 26³ = 676 × 26 = 17576.

#### 1.2.4 Approximation

**What it is:** Replacing awkward numbers by nearby friendly ones to get an answer quickly when the options are well separated.

**How to identify it**

- The question says "approximately", shows ≈ or "?", and the numbers are long decimals.
- Options are far apart (not 1451 versus 1452).

**How to solve it**

- Round each number to one or two significant figures, keep the same operations, calculate, and pick the closest option.
- Use friendly fractions: 24.9% ≈ 1/4, 33.2% ≈ 1/3, 12.4% ≈ 1/8.
- Avoid rounding when you subtract two nearly equal numbers; the error becomes large.

**Example 1.** Estimate 49.8 × 20.1 ÷ 9.9. **Solution.** Round to 50 × 20 ÷ 10. 50 × 20 = 1000, and 1000 ÷ 10 = 100. The answer is about 100.

**Example 2.** Estimate 39.97% of 2499 + 14.9% of 1199. **Solution.** 39.97% ≈ 40% and 2499 ≈ 2500, giving 1000. 14.9% ≈ 15% and 1199 ≈ 1200, giving 180. Total ≈ 1180.

#### 1.3.1 Basic percentage

**What it is:** Percent means "per hundred". x% of N = (x/100) × N.

**How to identify it**

- "What percent of…", "x% of a number", "is what percent of", comparison of two quantities.
- Election and exam-marks questions that give percentages of a total.

**How to solve it**

- x% of N = x × N / 100.
- A is what percent of B = (A / B) × 100.
- Learn the fraction forms: 1/2 = 50%, 1/3 = 33.33%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 = 16.67%, 1/7 = 14.28%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/10 = 10%, 1/11 = 9.09%, 1/12 = 8.33%.
- x% of y = y% of x, so pick whichever is easier.

**Example 1.** Find 18% of 450, and say what percent 63 is of 350. **Solution.** 18% of 450 = 0.18 × 450 = 81. 63 ÷ 350 × 100 = 18%.

**Example 2.** A candidate gets 45% of the votes and loses by 600 votes to the only other candidate. How many votes were cast? **Solution.** The other candidate gets 55%. The gap is 55% − 45% = 10%. 10% of the total = 600, so the total = 6000.

#### 1.3.2 Percentage change

**What it is:** How much a quantity has increased or decreased, expressed as a percentage of the original value.

**How to identify it**

- "Increased by x%", "what is the percentage increase/decrease", "A is x% more than B".
- Price rise and consumption cut questions.

**How to solve it**

- % change = (change ÷ original) × 100. The original is always the denominator.
- New value = original × (100 ± x)/100.
- If A is x% more than B, then B is 100x/(100 + x) % less than A.
- To keep expenditure the same after a price rise of x%, consumption must fall by 100x/(100 + x) %.

**Example 1.** Sugar becomes 25% costlier. By what percent must a family cut its use to keep the spending the same? **Solution.** Reduction = 100 × 25 / (100 + 25) = 20%.

**Example 2.** A's salary is 20% more than B's. By what percent is B's salary less than A's? **Solution.** Reduction = 100 × 20 / (100 + 20) = 16.67% (that is, 1/6).

#### 1.3.3 Successive percentages

**What it is:** Two or more percentage changes applied one after another. The net effect is not the simple sum of the changes.

**How to identify it**

- "Increased by 10% and then by 20%", "first increased, then decreased", repeated discounts or growth.
- Change in the area of a figure when its sides change by percentages.

**How to solve it**

- Net % change = a + b + ab/100, using + for an increase and − for a decrease.
- Or multiply the factors: +10% then +20% is 1.10 × 1.20 = 1.32, a 32% increase.
- For three changes, combine the first two, then combine the result with the third.

**Example 1.** A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the net change? **Solution.** Net = 20 − 20 + (20)(−20)/100 = −4%. The price is 4% lower. (Check: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.) **Example 2.** The side of a square is increased by 10%. What happens to its area? **Solution.** Area depends on the side twice: 10 + 10 + (10 × 10)/100 = 21%. The area increases by 21%.

#### 1.3.4 Population & depreciation

**What it is:** Growth or decline at a fixed percent per period compounds, because each period works on the new value.

**How to identify it**

- "Population increases by x% per year", "value of a machine depreciates at x% per annum", "after n years", "n years ago".

**How to solve it**

- Growth: final = P × (1 + r/100)ⁿ.
- Depreciation: final = P × (1 − r/100)ⁿ.
- If the rate changes each year, multiply the separate factors.
- To find an earlier value, divide by the factor instead of multiplying.

**Example 1.** A town has 20,000 people and grows 10% per year. Population after 2 years? **Solution.** 20000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 24,200.

**Example 2.** A machine costing ₹1,00,000 depreciates 10% every year. Its value after 3 years? **Solution.** 1,00,000 × 0.9³ = 1,00,000 × 0.729. Value = ₹72,900.

#### 1.4.1 Ratio

**What it is:** A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind by division. The ratio a : b is the fraction a/b.

**How to identify it**

- "Divide ₹X in the ratio…", "A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, find A : B : C".
- "The ratio changes when the same amount is added to both".

**How to solve it**

- To divide N in the ratio a : b, the shares are a/(a+b) × N and b/(a+b) × N.
- Write the quantities as ak and bk and use the conditions to find k.
- To join A : B and B : C, make the B terms equal using their LCM, then read off A : B : C.
- Compound ratio = product of the first terms : product of the second terms.

**Example 1.** If A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, find A : B : C. **Solution.** B is 3 in the first ratio and 4 in the second. The LCM of 3 and 4 is 12. A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15. So A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15.

**Example 2.** Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. When 10 is added to each, the ratio becomes 5 : 7. Find the numbers. **Solution.** Let the numbers be 3k and 5k. Then (3k + 10)/(5k + 10) = 5/7. 21k + 70 = 25k + 50, so 4k = 20 and k = 5. The numbers are 15 and 25. Check: 25/35 = 5/7.

#### 1.4.2 Proportion

**What it is:** Proportion is the equality of two ratios: a : b = c : d. The product of the extremes equals the product of the means, so ad = bc.

**How to identify it**

- "Find the fourth proportional", "third proportional", "mean proportional between".
- "If 6 pens cost ₹90, find the cost of 10 pens" (a unitary-method proportion).

**How to solve it**

- Fourth proportional to a, b, c = bc/a.
- Third proportional to a and b = b²/a.
- Mean proportional between a and b = √(ab).
- For unitary problems, find the value of one unit, then multiply.

**Example 1.** Find the mean proportional between 4 and 36, and the third proportional to 6 and 12. **Solution.** Mean proportional = √(4 × 36) = √144 = 12. Third proportional to 6 and 12 = 12²/6 = 24.

**Example 2.** If 6 pens cost ₹90, what do 10 pens cost? **Solution.** One pen costs 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15. Ten pens cost 10 × 15 = ₹150.

#### 1.4.3 Direct & inverse variation

**What it is:** Two quantities vary directly if they rise and fall together (y/x stays constant). They vary inversely if one rises as the other falls (x × y stays constant).

**How to identify it**

- Direct: cost and quantity, distance and time at a fixed speed, work done and number of workers.
- Inverse: men and days for the same job, speed and time for the same distance.
- Several linked quantities (men, hours per day, days) use the chain method.

**How to solve it**

- Direct: x₁/y₁ = x₂/y₂.
- Inverse: x₁ × y₁ = x₂ × y₂.
- Chain: men × hours × days is proportional to the work done. Compare the two situations.

**Example 1.** 12 men build a wall in 20 days. How many days will 15 men take? **Solution.** More men means fewer days (inverse): 12 × 20 = 15 × d. d = 240 ÷ 15 = 16 days.

**Example 2.** 5 men working 8 hours a day make 400 items in 10 days. How many items do 8 men make working 5 hours a day for 12 days? **Solution.** Man-hours in the first case = 5 × 8 × 10 = 400, which gives 400 items, so 1 item per man-hour. Man-hours in the second case = 8 × 5 × 12 = 480. Items = 480.

#### 1.4.4 Componendo & dividendo

**What it is:** A shortcut: if a/b = c/d then (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d).

**How to identify it**

- Equations such as (x + y)/(x − y) = 7/3 where you need x : y.
- Expressions where both a sum and a difference of the same two terms appear on top and bottom.

**How to solve it**

- Componendo: (a + b)/b = (c + d)/d. Dividendo: (a − b)/b = (c − d)/d.
- Combined: (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d).
- Read it backwards too: if (P + Q)/(P − Q) = m/n then P/Q = (m + n)/(m − n).

**Example 1.** If (x + y)/(x − y) = 7/3, find x : y. **Solution.** Using the shortcut in reverse: x/y = (7 + 3)/(7 − 3) = 10/4 = 5/2. Check: x = 5, y = 2 gives 7/3. **Example 2.** If (3a + 2b)/(3a − 2b) = 5/3, find a : b. **Solution.** 3a/2b = (5 + 3)/(5 − 3) = 8/2 = 4. So 3a = 8b and a/b = 8/3. Check: a = 8, b = 3 gives (24 + 6)/(24 − 6) = 30/18 = 5/3.

#### 1.5.1 Simple average

**What it is:** The average (mean) is the sum of the values divided by how many there are.

**How to identify it**

- "Average of…", "mean", "average age of a class", "the average of five numbers is…".
- Missing value or wrong value found later.

**How to solve it**

- Average = Sum ÷ Number of items, so Sum = Average × Number of items.
- For consecutive numbers or an arithmetic progression, average = (first + last)/2 = the middle term.
- Average of the first n natural numbers = (n + 1)/2. First n even numbers: n + 1. First n odd numbers: n.
- If every value rises by k, the average rises by k.

**Example 1.** The average of 5 numbers is 24. Four of them are 20, 22, 26 and 28. Find the fifth. **Solution.** Total = 5 × 24 = 120. The four known numbers add to 96. Fifth number = 120 − 96 = 24.

**Example 2.** The average of 7 consecutive numbers is 20. What is the largest? **Solution.** The middle (4th) number is the average, 20. The numbers run 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. The largest is 23.

#### 1.5.2 Weighted average

**What it is:** An average in which groups of different sizes count in proportion to their sizes.

**How to identify it**

- "Average of two sections combined", "average price of a mixture", "some items at one price, others at another".

**How to solve it**

- Weighted average = (n₁a₁ + n₂a₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂).
- The combined average always lies between the two group averages, nearer to the bigger group.
- Alligation shortcut: n₁ : n₂ = (a₂ − average) : (average − a₁).

**Example 1.** Class A has 40 students with average 70, and class B has 60 students with average 80. Find the combined average. **Solution.** Total marks = 40 × 70 + 60 × 80 = 2800 + 4800 = 7600. Average = 7600 ÷ 100 = 76.

**Example 2.** Rice at ₹40/kg is mixed with rice at ₹55/kg in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the average cost per kg? **Solution.** Cost of 5 kg = 2 × 40 + 3 × 55 = 80 + 165 = 245. Average = 245 ÷ 5 = ₹49/kg.

#### 1.5.3 Average speed

**What it is:** Average speed is total distance divided by total time. It is not the plain average of two speeds.

**How to identify it**

- "Goes at x km/h and returns at y km/h", "first half at…, second half at…", "average speed for the whole journey".

**How to solve it**

- Equal distances at speeds a and b: average speed = 2ab/(a + b).
- Equal times at speeds a and b: average speed = (a + b)/2.
- Unequal parts: total distance ÷ total time.

**Example 1.** A car travels to a town at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. Find its average speed. **Solution.** The distances are equal, so average = 2 × 60 × 40 ÷ (60 + 40) = 4800 ÷ 100. Average speed = 48 km/h. **Example 2.** A man travels for 2 hours at 30 km/h and then for 3 hours at 50 km/h. Find his average speed. **Solution.** Distance = 2 × 30 + 3 × 50 = 60 + 150 = 210 km. Time = 5 hours, so average speed = 210 ÷ 5 = 42 km/h.

#### 1.5.4 Replacement & addition problems

**What it is:** Working out how the average of a group changes when a member joins, leaves or is replaced, or finding the member's value from the change.

**How to identify it**

- "A new person joins and the average rises by…", "replaced by", "one student left".

**How to solve it**

- Replacement: value of new member − value of old member = (change in average) × (group size).
- Joining: new member's value = old average + (change in average) × (new group size).
- Leaving or any other case: write the total before and after; the difference is the member's value.

**Example 1.** The average weight of 8 men increases by 2.5 kg when a new man replaces one who weighs 60 kg. Find the weight of the new man. **Solution.** Total weight rises by 8 × 2.5 = 20 kg. New man = 60 + 20 = 80 kg.

**Example 2.** The average age of 10 people is 30. When an 11th person joins, the average becomes 31. Find the new person's age. **Solution.** Old total = 300. New total = 11 × 31 = 341. New person = 341 − 300 = 41 years.

#### 1.6.1 Present, past & future ages

**What it is:** Word problems that link people's ages at different times. Everyone's age changes by the same number of years, so the difference between two ages never changes.

**How to identify it**

- "x years ago", "after n years", "twice as old as", "sum of their ages".

**How to solve it**

- Let the youngest (or the one you are asked about) be x.
- Write each sentence as an equation. For a time shift of t years, add t (future) or subtract t (past) to every person's age.
- Solve the linear equation and check against every sentence.

**Example 1.** A father is 3 times as old as his son. After 12 years he will be twice as old. Find their present ages. **Solution.** Son = x, father = 3x. 3x + 12 = 2(x + 12), so 3x + 12 = 2x + 24 and x = 12. Son is 12 and father is 36.

**Example 2.** Ravi is 5 years older than Mohan. Four years ago Ravi was twice as old as Mohan. Find their ages now. **Solution.** Mohan = x, Ravi = x + 5. (x + 5) − 4 = 2(x − 4), so x + 1 = 2x − 8 and x = 9. Mohan is 9 and Ravi is 14. Check: four years ago they were 5 and 10.

#### 1.6.2 Ratio-based age problems

**What it is:** Ages are given as ratios, sometimes at two different times.

**How to identify it**

- "The ratio of their ages is 5 : 7", "after 8 years the ratio will be…".

**How to solve it**

- Present ages = ak and bk.
- Apply the time shift to each age, then use the second ratio or the stated sum or difference to find k.
- The difference (b − a)k stays the same at all times, which often gives a shortcut.

**Example 1.** The ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. Four years ago the sum of their ages was 52. Find their present ages. **Solution.** Present ages 5k and 7k. Four years ago the sum was 12k − 8 = 52. 12k = 60, so k = 5. Ages are 25 and 35. Check: four years ago 21 + 31 = 52.

**Example 2.** The ages of a mother and daughter are in the ratio 7 : 2. After 8 years the ratio will be 5 : 2. Find their present ages. **Solution.** Mother 7k, daughter 2k. (7k + 8)/(2k + 8) = 5/2. 14k + 16 = 10k + 40, so 4k = 24 and k = 6. Mother is 42 and daughter is 12. After 8 years they will be 50 and 20, which is 5 : 2.

#### 1.7.1 Simple partnership

**What it is:** Partners invest money for the same period and share the profit or loss in the ratio of their investments.

**How to identify it**

- "A and B start a business with ₹… and ₹…", "share the profit", all invested for the whole year.

**How to solve it**

- Profit ratio = ratio of investments.
- Each partner's share = (their parts ÷ total parts) × total profit.
- If one share and the ratio are known, scale up to the total.

**Example 1.** A invests ₹30,000 and B invests ₹50,000. The profit is ₹24,000. Find each share. **Solution.** Ratio = 3 : 5, total 8 parts, 1 part = ₹3,000. A gets 3 × 3000 = ₹9,000 and B gets 5 × 3000 = ₹15,000.

**Example 2.** Three partners invest ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹50,000. C's share of the profit is ₹15,000. Find the total profit. **Solution.** Ratio = 2 : 3 : 5, total 10 parts. C holds 5 parts = ₹15,000. One part = ₹3,000, so total profit = 10 × 3000 = ₹30,000.

#### 1.7.2 Compound partnership

**What it is:** Partners invest different amounts for different lengths of time, or change their capital. The profit is shared in the ratio of (capital × time).

**How to identify it**

- "B joins after 4 months", "A withdraws ₹… at the end of 6 months", different time periods.

**How to solve it**

- Profit ratio = capital₁ × months₁ : capital₂ × months₂ : …
- If a partner's capital changes, add up capital × months for each separate period.
- Then divide the profit in that ratio.

**Example 1.** A invests ₹6,000 for the whole year and B invests ₹8,000 for 9 months. In what ratio is the profit shared? **Solution.** A: 6000 × 12 = 72,000. B: 8000 × 9 = 72,000. Ratio = 1 : 1. **Example 2.** A starts a business with ₹5,000. After 4 months B joins with ₹6,000. The profit at the end of the year is ₹5,400. Find each share. **Solution.** A: 5000 × 12 = 60,000. B: 6000 × 8 = 48,000. Ratio = 5 : 4. One part = 5400 ÷ 9 = ₹600. A gets ₹3,000 and B gets ₹2,400.

#### 1.7.3 Working vs. sleeping partner

**What it is:** A working partner manages the business and is paid a commission or salary before the profit is shared. A sleeping partner only invests money.

**How to identify it**

- "A is a working partner and gets 10% of the profit for managing", "B is a sleeping partner", "salary".

**How to solve it**

- Deduct the commission or salary from the total profit first.
- Divide the remaining profit in the ratio of capital × time.
- The working partner's total = commission (or salary) + investment share.

**Example 1.** A (working) and B (sleeping) invest ₹40,000 and ₹60,000. A receives 10% of the profit for managing. The profit is ₹20,000. Find A's total. **Solution.** Commission = 10% of 20,000 = ₹2,000. Remaining = ₹18,000, shared 2 : 3. A's share = 7,200 and B's share = 10,800. A's total = 2,000 + 7,200 = ₹9,200.

**Example 2.** A manages the business for a salary of ₹1,000 a month and invests ₹20,000. B invests ₹30,000. The yearly profit before salary is ₹32,000. Find what each receives. **Solution.** Annual salary = 12 × 1000 = ₹12,000. Remaining profit = ₹20,000, shared 2 : 3. A's share = 8,000 and B's share = 12,000. A receives 12,000 + 8,000 = ₹20,000 in all, and B receives ₹12,000.

#### 1.8.1 Cost price, selling price, profit & loss

**What it is:** Cost price (CP) is what the seller pays; selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays. Profit = SP − CP, Loss = CP − SP.

**How to identify it**

- "Gain %", "loss %", "sold at a profit of", "find the cost price".

**How to solve it**

- Profit % = (Profit ÷ CP) × 100 and Loss % = (Loss ÷ CP) × 100. Percentages are on CP unless the question says otherwise.
- SP = CP × (100 + P)/100 for a profit, CP × (100 − L)/100 for a loss.
- CP = SP × 100/(100 + P) or SP × 100/(100 − L).
- If two articles are sold at the same price, one at a gain of p% and the other at a loss of p%, there is always a loss of p²/100 %.

**Example 1.** An article bought for ₹800 is sold for ₹920. Find the profit percent. **Solution.** Profit = 920 − 800 = ₹120. Profit % = 120 ÷ 800 × 100 = 15%.

**Example 2.** A shopkeeper gains 5% by selling a bag for ₹1,260. At what price must he sell it to gain 8%? **Solution.** CP = 1260 × 100/105 = ₹1,200. SP at 8% gain = 1200 × 1.08 = ₹1,296.

#### 1.8.2 Discount & marked price

**What it is:** The marked price (MP) is the price printed on the article. A discount is a reduction on the marked price, so SP = MP − discount.

**How to identify it**

- "Marked at", "list price", "discount of x%", "after allowing a discount", "marked up by".

**How to solve it**

- Discount % is always on MP, while profit % is on CP.
- SP = MP × (100 − d)/100.
- MP = CP × (100 + P)/(100 − d), which links marked price, profit and discount.
- Start with CP = 100 when percentages are given and no amounts.

**Example 1.** A shopkeeper marks a watch 40% above cost and allows a 25% discount. Find his profit percent. **Solution.** Take CP = 100. MP = 140. SP = 140 × 0.75 = 105. Profit = 5%.

**Example 2.** A dealer's cost is ₹45,000. What should he mark the item at so that, after a 10% discount, he still gains 15%? **Solution.** MP = 45000 × 1.15 ÷ 0.9 = 51,750 ÷ 0.9. MP = ₹57,500.

#### 1.8.3 Successive discounts

**What it is:** Two or more discounts allowed one after another. Together they equal one smaller discount than the simple sum.

**How to identify it**

- "Successive discounts of 20% and 10%", "discount series", "equivalent single discount".

**How to solve it**

- Net discount % = a + b − ab/100.
- Or multiply the factors: 20% and 10% give 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so the net discount is 28%.
- The order of the discounts does not change the final price.

**Example 1.** Find the single discount equal to successive discounts of 20% and 10%. **Solution.** Net = 20 + 10 − (20 × 10)/100 = 30 − 2. Single discount = 28%.

**Example 2.** A TV is marked ₹50,000 and is sold after successive discounts of 10% and 20%. Find the price paid. **Solution.** 50,000 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 50,000 × 0.72. Price = ₹36,000.

#### 1.8.4 Dishonest dealings

**What it is:** A seller makes extra profit by using a false weight or measure, either alone or on top of a markup.

**How to identify it**

- "Uses a weight of 900 g for 1 kg", "sells at cost price but uses a false weight", "claims to sell at cost".

**How to solve it**

- If sold at cost price: Gain % = (true weight − false weight) ÷ false weight × 100.
- Equivalent factor = true weight ÷ false weight.
- If there is also a markup, multiply the factors: total factor = (true ÷ false) × (1 + markup). Gain % = factor − 1 (as a percent).

**Example 1.** A shopkeeper sells at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find his gain percent. **Solution.** He gives 900 g but charges for 1000 g. Gain = 100 ÷ 900 × 100. Gain % = 11.11%.

**Example 2.** A trader uses an 800 g weight for 1 kg and also sells at 20% above cost. Find his total gain percent. **Solution.** False-weight factor = 1000 ÷ 800 = 1.25. Markup factor = 1.2. Total factor = 1.25 × 1.2 = 1.5, so the gain is 50%.

#### 1.9.1 Simple interest

**What it is:** Interest calculated only on the original sum (principal), at the same amount every year.

**How to identify it**

- "Simple interest", "per annum" with no mention of compounding, "in how many years will it double or triple".

**How to solve it**

- SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, and Amount = P + SI.
- Convert months to years (9 months = 0.75 year).
- A sum doubles when R × T = 100; triples when R × T = 200.

**Example 1.** Find the simple interest on ₹8,000 at 7.5% per annum for 4 years. **Solution.** SI = 8000 × 7.5 × 4 ÷ 100 = 8000 × 30 ÷ 100. SI = ₹2,400.

**Example 2.** At what simple interest rate will a sum become three times itself in 10 years? **Solution.** Interest needed = 2P, so 2P = P × R × 10 ÷ 100. R = 20% per annum.

#### 1.9.2 Compound interest

**What it is:** Interest earned on the principal plus the interest already added in earlier periods.

**How to identify it**

- "Compound interest", "compounded annually, half-yearly or quarterly".

**How to solve it**

- Amount = P × (1 + R/100)ⁿ, and CI = Amount − P.
- Half-yearly compounding: use rate R/2 and 2n periods. Quarterly: R/4 and 4n periods.
- If the rate differs each year, multiply (1 + r/100) for each year.

**Example 1.** Find the compound interest on ₹10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years. **Solution.** Amount = 10000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 12,100. CI = 12,100 − 10,000 = ₹2,100.

**Example 2.** Find the amount on ₹16,000 at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly, for 1 year. **Solution.** Rate per half-year = 10%, number of periods = 2. Amount = 16000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹19,360.

#### 1.9.3 Difference between CI and SI

**What it is:** For 2 and 3 years the gap between compound and simple interest on the same sum has a ready formula.

**How to identify it**

- "The difference between the compound and simple interest is ₹…", "find the sum".

**How to solve it**

- 2 years: CI − SI = P × (R/100)².
- 3 years: CI − SI = P × (R/100)² × (3 + R/100).
- Use the formula backwards to find P or R.

**Example 1.** The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 2 years at 5% per annum is ₹75. Find the sum. **Solution.** 75 = P × (0.05)² = P × 0.0025. P = 75 ÷ 0.0025 = ₹30,000.

**Example 2.** Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹10,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years. **Solution.** Difference = 10000 × (0.1)² × (3 + 0.1) = 10000 × 0.01 × 3.1 = ₹310. Check: SI = 3,000, CI = 10000 × (1.331 − 1) = 3,310.

#### 1.9.4 Installments

**What it is:** A loan or purchase price paid back in equal parts at regular intervals. Each installment covers the interest and part of the principal.

**How to identify it**

- "Payable in two equal annual installments", "cleared in equal yearly installments".

**How to solve it**

- Compound interest: the loan equals the present value of the installments. For 2 installments x at rate r: Loan = x/(1 + r) + x/(1 + r)².
- Simple interest: the installments paid early earn interest for the time left. For two yearly installments: x × (1 + r) + x = Loan × (1 + 2r).
- Find x from the equation.

**Example 1.** A loan of ₹21,000 is repaid in two equal annual installments at 10% compound interest. Find the installment. **Solution.** 21000 = x/1.1 + x/1.21 = x × (1.1 + 1)/1.21 = x × 2.1/1.21. x = 21000 × 1.21 ÷ 2.1 = ₹12,100.

**Example 2.** A loan of ₹3,500 at 10% simple interest is cleared in two equal yearly installments. Find the installment. **Solution.** Amount owed after 2 years = 3500 × 1.2 = 4,200. The first installment earns one year of interest: 1.1x + x = 4200, so 2.1x = 4200. x = ₹2,000.

#### 1.9.5 Effective rate of interest

**What it is:** The actual yearly rate you earn when interest is compounded more than once a year.

**How to identify it**

- "Effective annual rate", "equivalent annual rate", "compounded half-yearly or quarterly, what yearly rate is this the same as".

**How to solve it**

- Compounded k times a year at R%: effective rate = \[(1 + R/(100k))ᵏ − 1\] × 100.
- Half-yearly: k = 2. Quarterly: k = 4. Monthly: k = 12.
- The effective rate is always higher than the stated rate.

**Example 1.** Find the effective annual rate for 10% per annum compounded half-yearly. **Solution.** Growth factor = (1 + 0.05)² = 1.1025. Effective rate = 10.25%.

**Example 2.** Find the effective annual rate for 8% per annum compounded quarterly. **Solution.** Growth factor = (1.02)⁴ = 1.0824 (since 1.02² = 1.0404 and 1.0404² ≈ 1.0824). Effective rate ≈ 8.24%.

#### 1.10.1 Alligation rule

**What it is:** A quick way to find the ratio in which two ingredients of different price or strength must be mixed to get a required mean value.

**How to identify it**

- "In what ratio must … be mixed to get …", "mean price", "two varieties", percentage strength of solutions.

**How to solve it**

- Let the cheaper (lower) value be c, the dearer (higher) value d and the mean m.
- Quantity of cheaper : quantity of dearer = (d − m) : (m − c).
- The mean must lie between c and d. Cross-subtract along the diagonals and read the ratio.

**Example 1.** In what ratio must rice at ₹36/kg be mixed with rice at ₹42/kg to get a mixture worth ₹39.50/kg? **Solution.** Cheaper : dearer = (42 − 39.5) : (39.5 − 36) = 2.5 : 3.5. Ratio = 5 : 7. Check: (5 × 36 + 7 × 42) ÷ 12 = 474 ÷ 12 = 39.5. **Example 2.** In what ratio must a 30% alcohol solution be mixed with a 50% solution to get a 45% solution? **Solution.** Weaker : stronger = (50 − 45) : (45 − 30) = 5 : 15. Ratio = 1 : 3.

#### 1.10.2 Replacement of a mixture

**What it is:** Repeatedly taking out part of a liquid and replacing it with another liquid (usually water) dilutes the original liquid by a fixed fraction each time.

**How to identify it**

- "A vessel contains x litres of milk; y litres are removed and replaced with water; this is repeated n times".

**How to solve it**

- Original liquid left after n operations = x × (1 − y/x)ⁿ.
- Fraction of the original in the vessel = (1 − y/x)ⁿ.
- Water present = total − original liquid left.

**Example 1.** A 40-litre vessel is full of pure milk. 4 litres are removed and replaced with water, and the process is repeated once more. How much milk is left? **Solution.** Fraction left after each step = 1 − 4/40 = 0.9. Milk left = 40 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 32.4 litres.

**Example 2.** A container has 64 litres of milk. 16 litres are taken out and replaced with water, three times. Find the milk left and the milk : water ratio. **Solution.** Fraction left each time = 1 − 16/64 = 3/4. Milk left = 64 × (3/4)³ = 64 × 27/64 = 27 litres. Water = 64 − 27 = 37 litres, so milk : water = 27 : 37.

#### 1.11.1 Work-rate

**What it is:** If a person completes a job in n days, their one-day work is 1/n of the job. Rates of people working together add up.

**How to identify it**

- "A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days; together they take…".
- "A and B together finish in 8 days; A alone takes 12; find B alone".

**How to solve it**

- Rate of A = 1/a per day. Together: 1/a + 1/b = (a + b)/(ab), so days together = ab/(a + b).
- Work done in d days = d × rate.
- To find one worker from the pair, subtract: 1/b = 1/t − 1/a.
- If someone leaves or joins midway, calculate the work done in each stage and add.

**Example 1.** A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. How long will they take together? **Solution.** 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per day. They take 6 days.

**Example 2.** A can finish a job in 12 days. A and B together finish it in 8 days. How long does B take alone? **Solution.** B's rate = 1/8 − 1/12 = 3/24 − 2/24 = 1/24. B alone takes 24 days.

#### 1.11.2 Efficiency method

**What it is:** Take the total work as the LCM of the given days. Then each worker's efficiency (units of work per day) is a whole number, and the arithmetic becomes simple.

**How to identify it**

- Three or more workers with different times, workers leaving or joining, "work on alternate days".

**How to solve it**

- Total work = LCM of the days taken by the individuals.
- Efficiency = total work ÷ days taken.
- Add efficiencies for workers together. Time = total work ÷ combined efficiency.
- For alternate days, compute the work in one full cycle, count whole cycles, then handle the leftover.

**Example 1.** A, B and C can finish a job in 20, 30 and 60 days. How long will they take together? **Solution.** Total work = LCM(20, 30, 60) = 60 units. Efficiencies: A = 3, B = 2, C = 1 per day, together 6 per day. Time = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days.

**Example 2.** A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. How long does the job take? **Solution.** Total work = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units. A does 3 per day, B does 2 per day. Two-day cycle = 5 units. After 14 days (7 cycles) the work done is 35 units. One unit is left. The next day belongs to A, who needs 1/3 of a day. Total = 14 1/3 days.

#### 1.11.3 Work & wages

**What it is:** Payment for a job is shared in proportion to the work each person has done.

**How to identify it**

- "Total wages ₹…", "they work together and are paid", "share of each".

**How to solve it**

- Wage ratio = ratio of work done = efficiency × time.
- If they work for the same time, the ratio equals the ratio of efficiencies, which is the inverse of the ratio of their individual days.
- Find each person's share of the work first, then split the money in that ratio.

**Example 1.** A can finish a job in 6 days and B in 12 days. They work together on a job that pays ₹900. Find each share. **Solution.** Efficiency ratio = 1/6 : 1/12 = 2 : 1. A gets 2/3 × 900 = ₹600 and B gets ₹300.

**Example 2.** A and B can finish a job in 12 and 18 days. With C's help it is finished in 4 days and the wage is ₹1,800. Find each person's share. **Solution.** Rates: 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. All three together: 1/4 = 9/36, so C = 4/36 = 1/9 (9 days alone). Work done in 4 days: A = 12/36, B = 8/36, C = 16/36. Ratio = 3 : 2 : 4 (9 parts, ₹200 each). A gets ₹600, B gets ₹400 and C gets ₹800.

#### 1.11.4 Pipes & cisterns

**What it is:** Work-rate applied to tanks. An inlet pipe does positive work (fills), an outlet pipe or leak does negative work (empties).

**How to identify it**

- "A pipe can fill a tank in…", "an outlet empties it in…", "a leak", "all three pipes open together".

**How to solve it**

- Inlet rate = +1/t per hour, outlet rate = −1/t per hour.
- Net rate = sum of all rates. Time to fill = 1 ÷ net rate.
- A leak: if a pipe fills a tank in x hours but takes y hours (y \> x) because of a leak, the leak alone empties a full tank in xy/(y − x) hours.

**Example 1.** Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B in 8 hours. Pipe C empties it in 12 hours. If all are open, how long to fill the tank? **Solution.** Net rate = 1/6 + 1/8 − 1/12 = 4/24 + 3/24 − 2/24 = 5/24. Time = 24/5 = 4.8 hours.

**Example 2.** A tank fills in 5 hours. Because of a leak it takes 6 hours. How long does the leak take to empty a full tank? **Solution.** Time = 5 × 6 ÷ (6 − 5). The leak empties it in 30 hours.

#### 1.12.1 Basic formula

**What it is:** Distance = Speed × Time. All other problems in this topic are variations of this relation.

**How to identify it**

- "How far", "how long", "at what speed", "reaches late or early".

**How to solve it**

- Keep units consistent. km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5.
- For a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional: speeds in ratio a : b mean times in ratio b : a.
- Late/early problems: difference in times = d/s₁ − d/s₂.

**Example 1.** Convert 72 km/h into m/s and find the time to cover 500 m at this speed. **Solution.** 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s. Time = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 seconds.

**Example 2.** A man walking at 5 km/h reaches the office 20 minutes later than when he walks at 6 km/h. Find the distance. **Solution.** Time difference = 20 minutes = 1/3 hour. d/5 − d/6 = 1/3, so d/30 = 1/3 and d = 10 km.

#### 1.12.2 Relative speed

**What it is:** The speed of one moving object as seen from another. Speeds add when objects move towards or away from each other, and subtract when they move in the same direction.

**How to identify it**

- "Start from two places towards each other and meet", "overtakes", "chases", "catch up".

**How to solve it**

- Opposite directions: relative speed = S₁ + S₂.
- Same direction: relative speed = S₁ − S₂ (faster minus slower).
- Time to meet or catch up = gap (distance) ÷ relative speed.

**Example 1.** Two towns are 360 km apart. Two cars leave them at the same time, at 50 km/h and 70 km/h, towards each other. When do they meet? **Solution.** Relative speed = 50 + 70 = 120 km/h. Time = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours.

**Example 2.** A thief runs at 8 km/h. A policeman 100 m behind chases him at 10 km/h. How long to catch him? **Solution.** Relative speed = 10 − 8 = 2 km/h. Gap = 0.1 km. Time = 0.1 ÷ 2 = 0.05 hour = 3 minutes.

#### 1.12.3 Trains

**What it is:** Problems in which the length of the train matters. The train must cover its own length (and the length of whatever it crosses).

**How to identify it**

- "Crosses a pole, a man, a platform, a bridge, or another train".

**How to solve it**

- Pole or standing man: distance = length of train.
- Platform or bridge: distance = length of train + length of platform.
- Two trains crossing: distance = sum of both lengths; speed = sum of speeds (opposite) or difference (same direction).
- Convert km/h to m/s (× 5/18) when lengths are in metres.

**Example 1.** A 150 m train at 54 km/h crosses a 250 m platform. How long does it take? **Solution.** Speed = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s. Distance = 150 + 250 = 400 m. Time = 400 ÷ 15 = 26 2/3 seconds.

**Example 2.** Trains 120 m and 180 m long run at 60 km/h and 40 km/h in opposite directions. How long do they take to cross each other? **Solution.** Relative speed = 100 km/h = 100 × 5/18 = 250/9 m/s. Distance = 300 m. Time = 300 × 9 ÷ 250 = 10.8 seconds.

#### 1.12.4 Boats & streams

**What it is:** A boat's speed changes with the current of the stream. Moving with the stream (downstream) it is faster; against it (upstream) it is slower.

**How to identify it**

- "Boat", "stream", "upstream", "downstream", "speed in still water".

**How to solve it**

- Downstream speed D = b + s. Upstream speed U = b − s (b = boat in still water, s = stream).
- Boat speed b = (D + U)/2. Stream speed s = (D − U)/2.
- Total time for a round trip over distance d = d/(b + s) + d/(b − s).

**Example 1.** A boat goes 24 km downstream in 2 hours and returns in 3 hours. Find the speed of the boat and of the stream. **Solution.** Downstream speed = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 km/h. Upstream speed = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 km/h. Boat = (12 + 8)/2 = 10 km/h. Stream = (12 − 8)/2 = 2 km/h.

**Example 2.** A boat's speed in still water is 15 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. How long is a round trip to a place 36 km away? **Solution.** Downstream: 36 ÷ 18 = 2 hours. Upstream: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 hours. Total = 5 hours.

#### 1.12.5 Races & games

**What it is:** Races where one runner beats another by a distance or a time, or gives a head start.

**How to identify it**

- "A beats B by 20 m", "gives a start of", "dead heat", "wins by 10 seconds".

**How to solve it**

- If A beats B by x metres in a race of D metres, then when A has run D, B has run D − x. So speeds are in the ratio D : (D − x).
- Beating by time t: B would need t more seconds to finish.
- Chain the races: use the same moment of time and compare distances.

**Example 1.** In a 100 m race A beats B by 10 m, and B beats C by 10 m. By how much does A beat C? **Solution.** When A runs 100 m, B runs 90 m. When B runs 100 m, C runs 90 m. So when B runs 90 m, C runs 90 × 0.9 = 81 m. A beats C by 100 − 81 = 19 m. **Example 2.** A runs 1 km in 3 minutes and B in 3 minutes 20 seconds. By how much does A beat B? **Solution.** A takes 180 s. B takes 200 s for 1000 m, so in 180 s B covers 1000 × 180/200 = 900 m. A beats B by 100 m (or by 20 seconds).

#### 1.12.6 Circular tracks

**What it is:** Runners move round a closed loop. When they meet depends on their relative speed and the length of the track.

**How to identify it**

- "Circular track", "meet for the first time", "meet at the starting point", "round the track".

**How to solve it**

- Opposite directions: first meeting after L ÷ (S₁ + S₂).
- Same direction: first meeting after L ÷ (S₁ − S₂).
- To meet again at the starting point: take the LCM of the times each takes to complete one round.

**Example 1.** Two men start together from the same point of a 400 m track, running at 6 m/s and 4 m/s. When do they first meet if they run (a) in the same direction (b) in opposite directions? **Solution.** (a) Relative speed 6 − 4 = 2 m/s, so time = 400 ÷ 2 = 200 seconds. (b) Relative speed 6 + 4 = 10 m/s, so time = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 seconds.

**Example 2.** A and B run round a track, taking 12 minutes and 18 minutes per round. When will they next be together at the starting point? **Solution.** LCM(12, 18) = 36. They meet at the start after 36 minutes.

#### 1.12.7 Escalators

**What it is:** A person walks on a moving staircase. The person's own speed and the escalator's speed combine, so the steps counted differ from the visible steps.

**How to identify it**

- "Escalator", "moving staircase", "number of steps", "walks up (or down) the escalator".

**How to solve it**

- With the escalator: effective speed = person + escalator. Against it: person − escalator.
- Visible steps N = effective speed × time. Steps the person counts = own speed × time.
- If steps counted in two trips are given, use that time is proportional to the steps counted (same walking speed), and form two equations for N.

**Example 1.** A man counts 15 steps walking down a moving escalator and 60 steps walking up against it, at the same walking speed. Find the number of visible steps. **Solution.** Let the escalator carry e steps during the downward trip. Then N = 15 + e. Walking up takes 4 times as long (60 vs 15 steps), so the escalator moves 4e steps against him: N = 60 − 4e. 15 + e = 60 − 4e gives e = 9, so N = 24 steps.

**Example 2.** An escalator has 100 visible steps and moves up at 2 steps per second. A person climbs at 3 steps per second relative to the steps. Find the time taken and the steps the person counts. **Solution.** Effective speed = 3 + 2 = 5 steps per second. Time = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 seconds. Steps counted = 3 × 20 = 60.

#### 1.13.1 Linear equations

**What it is:** Equations in which the variable has power 1. They may have one variable or several (simultaneous equations).

**How to identify it**

- "Find x", "the sum of two numbers is… and their difference is…", "3 pens and 2 pencils cost…".

**How to solve it**

- One variable: collect the x terms on one side, numbers on the other.
- Two variables: elimination (match coefficients, add or subtract) or substitution.
- For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂: unique solution if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂; no solution if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂; infinitely many if all three ratios are equal.

**Example 1.** 3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₹36. 2 pens and 3 pencils cost ₹34. Find the price of a pen and a pencil. **Solution.** 3p + 2c = 36 and 2p + 3c = 34. Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 9p + 6c = 108 and 4p + 6c = 68. Subtract: 5p = 40, so p = 8. Then 24 + 2c = 36, so c = 6. Pen ₹8 and pencil ₹6. Check: 16 + 18 = 34.

**Example 2.** Solve (2x + 3)/5 = (x − 1)/2 + 1. **Solution.** Multiply by 10: 2(2x + 3) = 5(x − 1) + 10. 4x + 6 = 5x + 5, so x = 1. Check: left = 5/5 = 1, right = 0 + 1 = 1.

#### 1.13.2 Quadratic equations

**What it is:** Equations of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). They have two roots.

**How to identify it**

- An x² term, "find the roots", "nature of the roots", "sum and product of roots".
- "Compare x and y" questions where both come from quadratics.

**How to solve it**

- Factorise: find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term.
- Formula: x = \[−b ± √(b² − 4ac)\] / 2a.
- Sum of roots = −b/a. Product of roots = c/a.
- Discriminant D = b² − 4ac: D \> 0 two real roots, D = 0 equal roots, D \< 0 no real roots.

**Example 1.** Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0. **Solution.** Find two numbers with product 12 and sum 7: 3 and 4. (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 3 or x = 4.

**Example 2.** For 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 find the discriminant, and the sum and product of the roots. **Solution.** D = 25 − 24 = 1, which is positive, so the roots are real and different. Sum = 5/2 and product = 3/2. The roots are (5 ± 1)/4, that is 3/2 and 1.

#### 1.13.3 Inequalities

**What it is:** Statements using \<, \>, ≤ or ≥. Their solution is a range of values, not a single number.

**How to identify it**

- "Find the range of x", "how many integers satisfy", "solve the inequality".

**How to solve it**

- Solve as for an equation, but reverse the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
- Quadratic inequality: factorise, mark the roots on a number line, and test the regions.
- |x| \< a means −a \< x \< a. |x| \> a means x \< −a or x \> a.
- When counting integers, check whether each end is included (≤) or excluded (\<).

**Example 1.** Solve 5 − 2x \> 1. **Solution.** Subtract 5: −2x \> −4. Divide by −2 and reverse the sign: x \< 2. **Example 2.** How many integers satisfy x² − 3x − 4 ≤ 0? **Solution.** Factorise: (x − 4)(x + 1) ≤ 0. The product is non-positive between the roots: −1 ≤ x ≤ 4. Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 6 integers.

#### 1.13.4 Progressions (AP, GP, HP)

**What it is:** An arithmetic progression (AP) adds a constant difference, a geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio, and in a harmonic progression (HP) the reciprocals form an AP.

**How to identify it**

- "n-th term", "sum of first n terms", "common difference", "common ratio", "three numbers in AP/GP".

**How to solve it**

- AP: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Sₙ = n/2 × \[2a + (n − 1)d\] = n/2 × (first + last).
- GP: aₙ = a × rⁿ⁻¹. Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r \> 1. Infinite GP with |r| \< 1: S = a/(1 − r).
- HP: take reciprocals, solve as an AP, take reciprocals back. Harmonic mean of a and b = 2ab/(a + b).
- Three numbers in AP: a − d, a, a + d. In GP: a/r, a, ar.

**Example 1.** Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 3, 7, 11, … **Solution.** a = 3 and d = 4. S = 20/2 × \[2 × 3 + 19 × 4\] = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

**Example 2.** For the GP 2, 6, 18, … find the 6th term and the sum of the first 6 terms. **Solution.** a = 2 and r = 3. 6th term = 2 × 3⁵ = 2 × 243 = 486. Sum = 2 × (3⁶ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 729 − 1 = 728.

#### 1.13.5 Functions

**What it is:** A function f is a rule that gives exactly one output f(x) for each allowed input x.

**How to identify it**

- "f(x) = …, find f(3)", "composite function f(g(x))", "inverse function", "domain".

**How to solve it**

- Evaluate by substituting the value of x.
- Composite f(g(x)): work from the inside out. Order matters: f(g(x)) is usually not g(f(x)).
- Inverse: write y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, then swap the letters.
- Domain: exclude values that make a denominator zero or give the square root of a negative number.

**Example 1.** If f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x², find f(g(2)) and g(f(2)). **Solution.** g(2) = 4, so f(g(2)) = f(4) = 11. f(2) = 7, so g(f(2)) = g(7) = 49.

**Example 2.** Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 2)/5. **Solution.** Put y = (3x − 2)/5. Then 5y = 3x − 2, so x = (5y + 2)/3. Swapping letters: f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3. Check: f(1) = 1/5 and f⁻¹(1/5) = (1 + 2)/3 = 1.

#### 1.14.1 Fundamental counting principle

**What it is:** If one task can be done in m ways and a second task in n ways, doing both one after the other can be done in m × n ways (AND means multiply). If either task alone will do, the count is m + n (OR means add).

**How to identify it**

- "In how many ways can … and …", number of routes, outfits, passwords, numbers formed from digits.
- Digit questions with restrictions (no repetition, even number, first digit not zero).

**How to solve it**

- Break the job into stages and multiply the choices at each stage.
- Fill the most restricted place first (for an even number, fill the units digit first).
- When the cases split (such as units digit 0 versus non-zero), count each case separately and add.

**Example 1.** How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1 to 5 if no digit is repeated? **Solution.** Hundreds place: 5 choices. Tens place: 4 choices. Units place: 3 choices. Total = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

**Example 2.** How many 3-digit even numbers with all digits different can be formed from the digits 0 to 9? **Solution.** Fill the units place first, in two cases. Units digit 0: hundreds 9 choices, tens 8 choices, giving 72. Units digit 2, 4, 6 or 8 (4 choices): hundreds cannot be 0 or the used digit, so 8 choices; tens has 8 choices left (0 is allowed). That gives 4 × 8 × 8 = 256. Total = 72 + 256 = 328.

#### 1.14.2 Permutations

**What it is:** Permutations count arrangements in which the order matters. Selecting r items from n and arranging them: nPr = n!/(n − r)!.

**How to identify it**

- "Arrange", "seated in a row", "rank", "form words", "positions", "president and secretary".

**How to solve it**

- All n different items in a row: n!.
- Letters with repeats: n!/(p! × q! × …), where p, q are the counts of repeated letters.
- Items that must stay together: treat them as one block, arrange the blocks, then multiply by the internal arrangements.
- Items that must not be together: total arrangements − arrangements with them together.

**Example 1.** In how many ways can the letters of the word LEVEL be arranged? **Solution.** LEVEL has 5 letters, with L twice and E twice. Arrangements = 5!/(2! × 2!) = 120/4 = 30.

**Example 2.** In how many ways can 5 people sit in a row if two particular people must sit together? **Solution.** Treat the pair as one block, so there are 4 items to arrange: 4! = 24. The pair can swap inside the block in 2! = 2 ways. Total = 24 × 2 = 48.

#### 1.14.3 Combinations

**What it is:** Combinations count selections in which the order does not matter. nCr = n!/\[r!(n − r)!\] and nCr = nC(n − r).

**How to identify it**

- "Choose", "select", "committee", "team", "handshakes", "number of triangles or diagonals".

**How to solve it**

- Select from separate groups: multiply the combinations for each group.
- "At least one" = total selections − selections with none.
- Handshakes among n people: nC2. Diagonals of an n-sided polygon: nC2 − n.
- Choose first, arrange later: if the order matters afterwards, multiply the combinations by r!.

**Example 1.** A committee of 4 is to be formed from 6 men and 4 women, with exactly 2 women. In how many ways? **Solution.** Choose 2 women from 4: 4C2 = 6. Choose 2 men from 6: 6C2 = 15. Total = 6 × 15 = 90.

**Example 2.** A team of 3 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women and must include at least one woman. In how many ways? **Solution.** Total teams = 9C3 = 84. Teams with no woman (all men) = 5C3 = 10. Teams with at least one woman = 84 − 10 = 74.

#### 1.14.4 Circular permutations

**What it is:** Arrangements around a circle, where rotating everyone one place gives the same arrangement. n different items can be arranged in (n − 1)! ways.

**How to identify it**

- "Seated around a round table", "arranged in a circle", "necklace", "garland".

**How to solve it**

- n different people around a table: (n − 1)!. Fix one person to remove the rotations, then arrange the rest.
- Necklace or garland (it can be flipped over): (n − 1)!/2.
- Alternate arrangement of two groups: fix and arrange the first group circularly, then place the second group in the gaps.

**Example 1.** In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table? **Solution.** Fix one person. The other 5 can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways.

**Example 2.** In how many ways can 5 men and 5 women sit around a round table so that no two men are together? **Solution.** Seat the men first: (5 − 1)! = 24 ways. This leaves 5 gaps between them. Seat the 5 women in the gaps: 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2,880.

#### 1.14.5 Distribution problems

**What it is:** Counting the ways to share objects among people or to split them into groups.

**How to identify it**

- "Distribute", "in how many ways can 10 sweets be given to 3 children", "divide into groups".
- Check whether the objects are identical or different, and whether the groups are labelled.

**How to solve it**

- Identical objects among r different people, anyone may get none: (n + r − 1)C(r − 1).
- Identical objects, each person at least one: (n − 1)C(r − 1).
- Different objects among r people (any number each): rⁿ.
- Different objects into groups of sizes a, b, c: n!/(a! b! c!). If groups of equal size are unlabelled, also divide by the factorial of the number of equal groups.

**Example 1.** In how many ways can 10 identical sweets be given to 3 children so that each child gets at least one? **Solution.** Use (n − 1)C(r − 1) = 9C2. 9C2 = 36. **Example 2.** In how many ways can 6 different books be divided (a) among 3 people, 2 each, (b) into 3 unlabelled pairs? **Solution.** (a) 6!/(2! 2! 2!) = 720/8 = 90. (b) The 3 pairs are not labelled, so divide by 3! = 6: 90/6 = 15.

#### 1.15.1 Basic probability

**What it is:** Probability measures how likely an event is: P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (total number of equally likely outcomes). It lies between 0 and 1.

**How to identify it**

- "Probability", "chance", "at random", "likelihood".

**How to solve it**

- P(E) = n(E)/n(S).
- P(not E) = 1 − P(E). For "at least one", use 1 − P(none).
- When selecting items, count favourable and total outcomes with combinations.

**Example 1.** A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is red. **Solution.** Favourable = 5, total = 8. P(red) = 5/8.

**Example 2.** Two balls are drawn together from the same bag (5 red, 3 blue). Find the probability that both are red. **Solution.** Favourable = 5C2 = 10. Total = 8C2 = 28. P = 10/28 = 5/14.

#### 1.15.2 Independent & dependent events

**What it is:** Events are independent when one does not change the probability of the other (for example, with replacement). They are dependent when it does (for example, without replacement).

**How to identify it**

- "With replacement" or separate trials, such as two people each shooting: independent.
- "Without replacement" or "one after another from the same set": dependent.

**How to solve it**

- Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
- Either event: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). For mutually exclusive events there is nothing to subtract.
- Dependent: multiply the first probability by the new (changed) probability of the second.
- "At least one occurs" = 1 − P(none occurs).

**Example 1.** A hits a target with probability 1/3 and B with probability 1/4. Both fire once. Find the probability that the target is hit. **Solution.** P(both miss) = (1 − 1/3)(1 − 1/4) = 2/3 × 3/4 = 1/2. P(target hit) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.

**Example 2.** Two cards are drawn one after another, without replacement, from a pack of 52. Find the probability that both are aces. **Solution.** P(first ace) = 4/52. P(second ace after one removed) = 3/51. P = 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.

#### 1.15.3 Conditional probability

**What it is:** The probability of an event A when we already know that event B has happened: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B).

**How to identify it**

- "Given that", "if it is known that", "provided that", "what is the probability that it came from…".

**How to solve it**

- Shrink the sample space to B, then count how much of B is also A.
- Formula: P(A|B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(B).
- Bayes' theorem (reverse a condition): P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A)/P(B), where P(B) adds up all the ways B can happen.

**Example 1.** A die is rolled. Given that the result is even, find the probability that it is greater than 3. **Solution.** Even results: 2, 4, 6 (3 outcomes). Of these, greater than 3: 4 and 6 (2 outcomes). P = 2/3.

**Example 2.** Machine A makes 60% of the items and 2% of its items are defective. Machine B makes 40% and 5% of its items are defective. An item picked at random is defective. Find the probability that it came from B. **Solution.** P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. P(from B and defective) = 0.020. P(B | defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 5/8.

#### 1.15.4 Cards, dice & coins

**What it is:** Standard sample spaces that appear in many questions. You need to know them by heart to count quickly.

**How to identify it**

- "A pack of cards", "two dice", "three coins are tossed", "sum of the numbers".

**How to solve it**

- Coins: n coins give 2ⁿ outcomes. Exactly r heads: nCr ways.
- Two dice: 36 outcomes. Number of ways for sum 2 to 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
- Pack: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 26 red and 26 black, 12 face cards (J, Q, K), 4 aces.
- For "or" questions with overlap, subtract the common cards or outcomes.

**Example 1.** Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that the sum is 8. **Solution.** Favourable pairs: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), which is 5. P = 5/36.

**Example 2.** Three coins are tossed. Find the probability of exactly 2 heads. **Solution.** Total outcomes = 2³ = 8. Exactly 2 heads: 3C2 = 3 outcomes. P = 3/8.

**Example 3.** One card is drawn from a pack of 52. Find the probability that it is a king or a heart. **Solution.** 4 kings + 13 hearts − 1 king of hearts (counted twice) = 16 cards. P = 16/52 = 4/13.

#### 1.16.1 Lines & angles

**What it is:** The basic rules about angles formed by lines, including parallel lines cut by a transversal.

**How to identify it**

- "Parallel lines", "transversal", "complementary", "supplementary", "find the angle".

**How to solve it**

- Complementary angles add to 90°. Supplementary angles add to 180°. A linear pair adds to 180°.
- Vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles around a point add to 360°.
- Parallel lines with a transversal: corresponding angles equal, alternate angles equal, co-interior (same-side) angles add to 180°.
- Always put the unknown as x, write the relation, and solve.

**Example 1.** An angle is 20° more than its complement. Find the angle. **Solution.** Let the angle be x. Its complement is 90 − x. x = (90 − x) + 20, so 2x = 110 and x = 55°. **Example 2.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two co-interior angles are (3x + 10)° and (2x + 20)°. Find x and the angles. **Solution.** Co-interior angles add to 180°: 5x + 30 = 180, so x = 30. The angles are 100° and 80°.

#### 1.16.2 Triangles

**What it is:** A triangle has three sides and its angles add to 180°. Key topics are the Pythagoras theorem, area, similarity and special points (centroid, incentre, circumcentre).

**How to identify it**

- "Right-angled triangle", "area of a triangle with sides…", "similar triangles", "inradius", "median".

**How to solve it**

- Angle sum = 180°. An exterior angle = the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
- Pythagoras: a² + b² = c². Common triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25).
- Area = 1/2 × base × height. Heron: √\[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)\] with s = half the perimeter. Equilateral: (√3/4)a².
- Similar triangles: sides in proportion; ratio of areas = square of ratio of sides.
- Inradius = area ÷ s. Circumradius of a right triangle = half the hypotenuse. The centroid divides a median 2 : 1.

**Example 1.** Find the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. **Solution.** s = (13 + 14 + 15)/2 = 21. Area = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84 cm².

**Example 2.** Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 2 : 3. The smaller has area 20 cm². Find the area of the larger. **Solution.** Ratio of areas = 2² : 3² = 4 : 9. Larger area = 20 × 9/4 = 45 cm².

#### 1.16.3 Circles

**What it is:** A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance (radius) from a centre. Questions use chords, tangents, arcs, sectors and the angles they make.

**How to identify it**

- "Chord", "tangent", "arc", "sector", "angle subtended", "distance from the centre".

**How to solve it**

- Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr².
- Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr. Sector area = (θ/360) × πr².
- A perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Chord = 2√(r² − d²) at distance d from the centre.
- A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Tangents from one outside point are equal in length.
- The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. The angle in a semicircle is 90°.

**Example 1.** A chord 16 cm long is in a circle of radius 10 cm. Find its distance from the centre. **Solution.** The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving half-length 8 cm. d = √(10² − 8²) = √36 = 6 cm.

**Example 2.** Find the arc length and area of a sector with angle 72° in a circle of radius 10 cm (take π = 3.14). **Solution.** Fraction of the circle = 72/360 = 1/5. Arc length = 1/5 × 2 × 3.14 × 10 = 12.56 cm. Area = 1/5 × 3.14 × 100 = 62.8 cm².

#### 1.16.4 Quadrilaterals & polygons

**What it is:** Four-sided figures (square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium) and many-sided polygons, with their angle and area rules.

**How to identify it**

- "Regular polygon", "interior or exterior angle", "diagonals", "area of a rhombus or trapezium".

**How to solve it**

- Sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180°. Each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360°/n.
- Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
- Rhombus: diagonals bisect each other at right angles, area = 1/2 × d₁ × d₂. Parallelogram area = base × height. Trapezium area = 1/2 × (sum of parallel sides) × height.
- Rectangle diagonal = √(l² + b²). Square diagonal = a√2.

**Example 1.** Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. Find the number of sides and the sum of the interior angles. **Solution.** Number of sides = 360/30 = 12. Interior angle sum = (12 − 2) × 180 = 1800°.

**Example 2.** The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side and area. **Solution.** The diagonals bisect at right angles, giving half-diagonals 8 and 6. Side = √(8² + 6²) = 10 cm. Area = 1/2 × 16 × 12 = 96 cm².

#### 1.16.5 Coordinate geometry

**What it is:** Describing points and lines with coordinates (x, y) on a plane and using formulas to find distances, slopes and areas.

**How to identify it**

- Points such as A(2, 3), "distance between", "midpoint", "slope", "equation of a line", "area of a triangle with vertices…".

**How to solve it**

- Distance = √\[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²\]. Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
- Section formula, dividing in ratio m : n internally: ((m x₂ + n x₁)/(m + n), (m y₂ + n y₁)/(m + n)).
- Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
- Line: y = mx + c, or y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
- Area of a triangle = 1/2 × |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.

**Example 1.** Find the distance between (1, 2) and (7, 10), and the midpoint. **Solution.** Distance = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10. Midpoint = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6).

**Example 2.** Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 5). **Solution.** Area = 1/2 × |1(1 − 5) + 5(5 − 1) + 3(1 − 1)| = 1/2 × |−4 + 20 + 0| = 8. Check: base 4 and height 4 give 1/2 × 4 × 4 = 8.

#### 1.17.1 2D figures: area & perimeter

**What it is:** Area is the surface a flat figure covers; perimeter is the length of its boundary.

**How to identify it**

- "Area", "perimeter", "cost of fencing or carpeting", "a path around a garden", "wire bent into a shape".

**How to solve it**

- Rectangle: area = l × b, perimeter = 2(l + b). Square: a² and 4a. Triangle: 1/2 × b × h. Circle: πr² and 2πr.
- Parallelogram: b × h. Trapezium: 1/2 × (a + b) × h. Rhombus: 1/2 × d₁ × d₂.
- A path of uniform width: area of path = outer area − inner area.
- Cost = area × rate per unit area (carpet) or perimeter × rate per unit length (fencing).
- If a wire is reshaped, its length (perimeter) stays the same.

**Example 1.** A rectangular park 60 m by 40 m has a 2 m wide path running inside along its border. Find the area of the path. **Solution.** Inner rectangle = (60 − 4) × (40 − 4) = 56 × 36 = 2016 m². Outer = 60 × 40 = 2400 m². Path = 2400 − 2016 = 384 m².

**Example 2.** A circular wire of radius 14 cm is bent into a square. Find the side and the area of the square (π = 22/7). **Solution.** Length of wire = 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88 cm. Side = 88 ÷ 4 = 22 cm. Area = 22² = 484 cm².

#### 1.17.2 3D figures: surface area & volume

**What it is:** Surface area is the total area of the faces of a solid; volume is the space it occupies.

**How to identify it**

- "Volume", "capacity", "curved surface area", "melted and recast", "cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere".

**How to solve it**

- Cube: V = a³, TSA = 6a², diagonal = a√3. Cuboid: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), diagonal = √(l² + b² + h²).
- Cylinder: V = πr²h, CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h).
- Cone: V = 1/3 πr²h, CSA = πrl, slant height l = √(r² + h²).
- Sphere: V = 4/3 πr³, surface area = 4πr². Hemisphere: V = 2/3 πr³, TSA = 3πr².
- Melting and recasting: the volume stays the same, so equate the volumes.

**Example 1.** A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area (π = 22/7). **Solution.** Volume = 22/7 × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm³. TSA = 2 × 22/7 × 7 × (7 + 10) = 44 × 17 = 748 cm².

**Example 2.** A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 2 cm. How many small spheres are made? **Solution.** Volumes are in the ratio of the cubes of the radii. Number = (6/2)³ = 27.

#### 1.18.1 Ratios & identities
